title: May we see a hundred autumns; may the Sun purify us

words.context: Bhāskara: «तच्चक्षुस्स्थानीयं», ‘that which stands as the eye’

words.meaning: set in place by the god; good for the gods
may we rejoice, may we prosper

words.role: the last wish: to see the Sun for long

sandhi.rule: t before c becomes c; -uḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -ur
final m before a vowel is kept and joins it

samasa.meaning: set in place by the god; good for the gods

morphology.note: नन्दाम, मोदाम, भवाम, शृणवाम, प्रब्रवाम are subjunctives (‘let us …’), alternating with the optatives पश्येम, जीवेम, स्याम; all express a wish.

translation.literal: That eye, set by the god, bright, rising in the east — may we see a hundred autumns, may we live a hundred autumns, rejoice a hundred autumns, be glad a hundred autumns, flourish a hundred autumns, hear a hundred autumns, speak a hundred autumns, be unconquered a hundred autumns, and long see the Sun.
translation.readable: There rises in the east that bright eye, set in place by the god. By its grace may we see for a hundred years, live for a hundred years, rejoice and be glad for a hundred years, flourish, hear and speak for a hundred years, stand undefeated for a hundred years — and long behold the Sun.

words.meaning: from the flood, from the ocean

words.gram: present middle participle, m. nom. sg.

words.meaning: of the waters, of the expanse

words.context: Bhāskara reads it as a locative: «मध्यान् मध्ये»

words.role: correlative of yaḥ, subject of punātu

words.meaning: the bull; the strong one, the giver of rain

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a vowel other than a loses its visarga; t before m becomes n
-aḥ + a becomes -o ’; t before v becomes d
t before a nasal becomes n

morphology.note: सरिर is the Vedic form of सलिल, ‘waters’ (r for l).

translation.literal: He who has risen from the great flood, shining forth, from the middle of the waters — may he, the bull, the red-eyed Sun, the wise, purify me with his mind.
translation.readable: He who rose shining from the great ocean, from the midst of the waters — may that Sun, the mighty, the red-eyed, the wise, purify me with his favour.

meaning: The close of the midday upasthāna, from the fourth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (4.42.5 in the muralīdhara text; Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara comments on it in his seventh prapāṭhaka, among the Pravargya mantras). The first part is the long prayer for a full life: the worshipper looks at the Sun rising in the east, the eye set in place by the god, and asks to see, live, rejoice, flourish, hear and speak, and stand unconquered, ‘for a hundred autumns’. The second part asks the Sun, risen from the great ocean, to purify the one who prays. The Ṛgveda has the beginning of the first part (7.66.16) but not the long series of wishes or the second verse.
in_the_rite: Midday sūryopasthāna, the fourth and fifth of its mantras, recited standing and facing the Sun after ud u tyam and citraṃ devānām. The Mylapore prayoga writes the series line by line (पश्येम शरदः शतम्। जीवेम …), and gives no separate viniyoga; the upasthāna’s viniyoga is the one stated for ā satyena (vin-a-satyena).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara reads each wish as a wish for whole faculties: «तत्प्रसादाद् अविकलचक्षुषः स्यास», ‘by its grace may we have unimpaired eyes’ — «शृणवाम अविकलश्रोत्रा भवाम», ‘unimpaired ears’; ‘unconquered’ is «अनभिभूतास्स्याम». The eye is set in place by the god, the supreme Self: «देवहितं देवेन परमात्मना स्थापितं».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: On the second verse: the Sun rises every day from the great ocean and from the middle of the sky — «यो महतोऽर्णवान् नित्यम् उदगाद् उद्गच्छति सरिरस्य अन्तरिक्षस्य मध्यान् मध्ये» — and, as the inner Self, purifies with his favour: «विपश्चित् सर्वज्ञो ऽन्तरात्मा भूत्वा», «मनसा सानुग्रहेण पुनातु शोधयतु».

notes.label: linguistic
notes.text: The Ṛgveda (7.66.16) reads «तच्चक्षुर्देवहितं शुक्रमुच्चरत् । पश्येम शरदः शतं जीवेम शरदः शतम्», without पुरस्तात् and without the rest of the series.

notes.label: direct
notes.text: The second witness of the Āraṇyaka, the gaṇeśvara text, is an OCR transcription with many slips (मादाम for मोदाम, सूर्यन्तशे for सूर्यं दृशे); they are listed in corrections.json as witness errors and do not affect the text.
